The Death of Dick Long is one of the most American films out there. I feel like what is "culturally American," has become so universal that it may not even be recognized as "distinctly" American. Smaller, more intimate pictures that explore the dynamics of a small town, the aside reference to a politician nobody likes. Our folktales are about Hollywood, the legend of Brando.

Honestly? It's been almost 25 years since September 11th and the United States' disastrous response. However, the cultural scars and social consequences will probably continue to haunt us until some huge, like, World War III-level event. 

We Americans simply are no longer proud of our country, we take our privilege for granted, and we make a lot of post-modernist stuff that mistakes self-loathing for thoughtful critique. 

And before you people come jumping down my throat—I'm not saying that we should be making every movie to be happy and gun-ho about "Murica, I'm just observing that we clearly aren't interested in showing national pride and that having nothing to root for is making us collectively depressed.

Side note: A while back, I read a very interesting essay pointing out how the Batman films are always reflections of contemporary American attitudes, and I think that's spot on. Sure, the 1989 Batman was gothic, but it had glamor and camp and Bruce Wayne was a little quirky. He could have girlfriends and the villains of Gotham City were whimsical. By 2005, Batman was more focused, militarized, and Bruce Wayne has only one last hope for happiness in his sole love interest, who later dies. The villains were more or less terrorists. And by 2022, Batman is just a depressed loner who prowls the streets in anger, and his villain is an online extremist and a corrupt justice system.

Because lots of jobs have become professionalized. There was a time when someone could start working as a copy boy at a newspaper and work their way up to reporter and then columnist. Or someone could be a runner on a trading desk and work their way up to trader. Today, if you want to end up in those jobs you need to go to the right schools and get the right credentials.

I would put forward there's an intentional "blandification" of anything that's trying to reach a global market, which most American films now are. They're also intensely profit-motivated, which doubles down the effects of this somewhat. The producers will get involved if they don't think a reference is going to land with a certain audience, so anything that's deemed too specific to America and not essential to the concept gets cut. The same goes for jokes that everyone isn't going to get instantly, which is why humour is so mediocre in modern American films. It turns out these details were a bit part of what gave the old films their character, hence the blandification.

I'd say your observation applies mostly to large-scale blockbusters. Since those movies are designed for mass international appeal, most are stripped of cultural signifiers because theoretically it broadens their market share. 


However, another reason is the nature of present technology means that we don't share a monoculture anymore. Algorithms and private screens have almost completely replaced catered programming on television and the cinema. As such, cultural signifiers/references on mass scale rarely occur. Things like Demar Hamlin's cardiac arrest, the Will Smith slap, and the Titanic submarine are memorable events for many, but you could totally miss them because of the speed of the news cycle, or simply because a social media algorithm didn't think you'd find it interesting.


This means frames of reference are completely fucked across generations. A great example of this is how *Everything Everywhere All at Once* has an extended bit based of Ratatouille, which is a kids film that came out 16 years before. It's very telling that the filmmakers would reference a movie from their childhoods, as 2007-08 would be the last years before social media came completely ubiquitous, and took place of monoculture. As such, there's seemingly less "Americanisms" in movies because every person has their own private America on their phone, and you can't well reference all of them.

> I don’t think its an effort to reduce American culture but rather an emphasis on making films accessible to international markets.

I wonder if this was a misreading of what the international market wanted from American movies.

American movies and sitcoms didn't become popular cultural exports around the globe because they were just sweeping, culturally non-specific pieces of entertainment. People liked them because *were* American in feel, steeped with weird little references to cultural things people liked to learn about.

The key to international accessibility isn't dumbing down the cultural references, it's just about making the content literally accessible to people overseas. It's why K-Dramas and Anime have been having their moment in the sun (anime for many years longer than Hallyu stuff), while stuff like NHK dramas aren't.

What even is American culture right now? To answer that, imo, you need to examine why storytellers are historically older than they’ve ever really been, and why even those that do get in, either have massive concessions to do so etc. 

With that in mind, even with the perfectly observant young filmmaker, I don’t necessarily think they they want to reflect “American” culture, which, ironically, is actually a very distinctly American artistic theme in of itself. American film is also at a point where it’s been subject to portability as the point, rather than a byproduct of its quality, which has reflected on audiences and filmmakers alike as a consequence.

Yeah and Vietnam, combined with all the other negative headlines of the 1970s, gave us The Godfather, Taxi Driver, All The President’s Men, Klute, Dirty Hairy, Rocky, Star Wars, and many more. But eventually, Reagan came and we bounced back in the 1980s and through to the 90s. Love him or hate him now, he was one of the most popular presidents of all time and Americans found their pride restored.

Post 9/11, the closest we ever got to that was optimism around Obama’s election. We’ve had two failed wars, the Patriot Act, cratering blue collar opportunity, the Great Recession, echo chambers, political polarization, Trumpism, two years of socially disastrous lockdown, and countless mass shootings. IMO we’re never going to come together again unless faced with a major crisis, like an international war with established foreign powers.

You've touched on something important to me, so forgive the length of my response and perhaps the bitterness of it.

This is something I've been fighting against as a filmmaker, but it's also prevalent in the arts as a whole, to be honest; and it's a big, complicated problem. In graduate school I and others often encountered discouraging obstacles that were entirely a product of faculty bias and willing ignorance, and as such I've learned as a result that the way LA Rebellion filmmakers like Charles Burnett and Julie Dash were buried by Hollywood has not changed or improved in the slightest. The system is almost entirely risk averse; betting any amount of capital on a passion project, regardless of its cultural worth, is only getting more uncommon as Disney snatches up independent filmmakers to helm their next tentpole and A24 shifts to more commercial projects. Very few companies within the United States are willing to bat for something culturally significant, and grants are generally more accessible for documentary in my experience. Making work that says something is not in fashion, unfortunately.

Another component of that unwillingness to take risks is language; you'll sometimes see films that include dialogue that isn't in English, but the majority of festivals, internationally included, state English subtitles as a requirement, but most of the festivals that state their dedication to marginalized groups time after time have statistically screened international productions or films in English and not American made non-English cinema. We live in a country of staggering diversity, so it's rather depressing that ethnic filmmakers are often unable to finance, market and/or distribute their work to wider audiences if their films are not in English. Historically Asian directors such as Bong Joon-ho and Park Chan-wook felt that the only way to work their way into the American film industry was to direct English language cinema, and doing so had mixed results, depending on your perspective. The reason for this is that even now your average American audience considers subtitles a nuisance, so the likelihood that non-English films will find success is slim in a studio's eyes, forcing filmmakers of diverse cultural backgrounds to change their work accordingly, potentially at the expense of valuable storytelling that could inspire real innovation. 

If that wasn't enough, it doesn't help that many of the contenders for awards every year are homogenized in many ways, whether it's the expensive camera packages they shoot with outside the budgets of many independent films, the actors involved and the reputation they have, or the fact that most international films are rarely nominated outside of their designated category. A film like "The Creator" is somewhat demonstrative of how little something like a camera matters, but it's arguably still working within the boundaries of Hollywood's preferences when it shoots on glass that's two times more expensive than my car. Even the idea of the low budget film of staggering quality pioneered by filmmakers like Barbara Loden or John Cassavetes is long gone from American theaters; the majority of independent cinema costs over 2 million dollars while studio films cost 30 times that, if not more. I still remember when "The Lighthouse" released in 2019 how many times I heard someone say it looked like a "student film," but I've not seen many student films of that quality, and I've seen a lot. Were Bergman or Antonioni's films "student films" too? 

Factor in the grueling work many crew members face from pre to post production and you have a system that is almost broken beyond repair, and you can certainly argue that the tools for filmmaking allow for a more democratic experience than ever before as prices on competitive options drop, but monetizing your film through YouTube or paying annual fees for an aggregator like Filmhub hardly makes such an endeavor worthwhile, let alone profitable. Someone somewhere with more money than they know what to do with is sitting in a room at a large table with other rich executives who have zero interest in the cultural benefits of cinema, but they'll tell you otherwise, and they will ensure that American film stays franchised.

Finally, most American audiences have reinforced the status quo; I can count on one hand the amount of people I've met that aren't creatives that have an interest in art films, nor have I met many that wouldn't rather play it safe watching the most recent Marvel film if they had a choice. I can't even get my family or friends to watch a David Lynch film on streaming, but they're happy to go watch something like "Thor: Love and Thunder" and spend extra on drinks and snacks. I went to the same graduate school as Hong Sang-soo and Apichatpong Weerasethakul and I've stood next to the latter for an hour, but my three short films have been declined at least 12 times each by various festivals and I've had to delay production of my feature films indefinitely since no one has seen them and I've yet to receive any of the grants I've spent countless hours applying for. My point is this: as long as people emphasize the value of popcorn cinema, things will not change. People like myself might never get to show you an American story with the authenticity you want to see.

TLDR: Until people stop spending money on live action Disney or Spiderman to line the pockets of executives who don't care about art, American film will not be culturally significant.

I disagree with you (respectfully) on two fronts:

I think the 70’s New Hollywood was both profoundly American and also a response to international movements in cinema, meaning I don’t think whether people are proud or upbeat really factors into it; the national mood was sour in the 70’s but there was a complex web of confluences that made the decade what it was.

I also don’t think the national mood has been comparably sour for the entire last 20 years, and I also don’t take quite the same bleak line of reasoning. Things are strained and people’s moods of late are certainly sour (comparable to the 70’s) but the world and nation as a whole still trends positively in innumerable metrics. Everything you list is true and valid (and politics of the last decade have certainly been more toxic than the preceding 50ish years) but I don’t think American culture or art is really that markedly bleaker than any other period experiencing an ebb.

I’ll concede my assessment of the 70s was a bit blunt, but I stand by my belief that 21st century mainstream American cinema is frequently bleak, or at the very least much more morally grey than the 80s–90s. 

The happiest mainstream blockbusters are superhero films that glorify individualism over community. Even many Disney movies have gone from supporting traditional values to being much more focused on their shallow girl boss brand.

Nowhere is this easier to see than if you compare Rey’s character arc to Luke’s. In the original trilogy, the highest level of morality through the Force is a high level of concern for community and harmony. In the prequels, we see the dark side of this, and Lucas was not remotely subtle about the political messages he was trying to pen. But when Disney got their hands on SW, all that was discarded in favor of Rey simply discovering what an amazing individual she can be—just like every other Disney protagonist of the last 20 years.

And then you have the popular trend of legacy sequels with worn-down characters and reboots that aim to make something darker and “more adult”.

So what mainstream movies actually promote happiness and community? I suppose the Avatar movies do this well, as did Top Gun: Maverick last year, and I hope that Barbie’s enormous success tells the studios that people do want movies where the message is that we can be great together.

This trend can be seen in music too; pop, rap, and rock have all gotten structurally simpler, but lyrically darker and more explicit (specifically with many more frequent references to mental illness) as the decades have rolled on.

I am aware that I’ve exclusively been talking about mainstream blockbusters, but I think that’s reasonable here because blockbusters are where you can reliably see into the collective social conscience (big fan of Krakauer for this reason). And apologies if my post comes off as overly grim, I’m just observing cinematic trends—not trying to actually say that we’re living in the worst of times.

Well, I think that there was a real turning point after we “won” the Cold War. There was no need to be so overt in promoting our own cultural exports because American culture became more of a worldwide default than before, when we were competing with the “second world” for that reach.

In addition, cinema aged and came into its own as a medium, and as that happened over time, the medium became the message. Films were no longer a vehicle to promote American art forms (detective stories, westerns, jazz, musicals, folk tales). Rather, films were themselves the American art form. Just by virtue of being a Hollywood film, movies were promoting American culture.

This but has been mentioned, but it’s a sort of “this is water” situation. Films have a language, a grammar. Most of the time that I speak, I don’t actively think “I’m speaking English.” It’s just so normal to me that I think of it as just speaking. Similarly, I don’t process American films as having American film grammar (cutting, coverage, acting styles), unless I just recently watched a foreign film that’s relatively unaffected by American media’s influence. Then I notice it.

If you look at the average Marvel film, sure it may not have a bunch of references to bits of American culture, but that’s because it is American culture. Superhero comics, Captain America, the idea that New York is the capital of the world. The idea that all interacting with aliens will be done by an American organization. It’s all very American. I’m sure it will feel far more American than it does now looking back in twenty years.

By comparison, many Japanese art forms predate cinema by hundreds of years. Cinema is one of America’s first art forms that it can really call it’s own (despite a big debt to Melies). So it is one of the oldest American arts. Japanese film tends to quote these older traditions, but American film has fewer older traditions to quote from, and many of those it used to were eventually rendered obsolete by it. To take this American art form and make it Japanese, Japanese film tends to take inspiration from Noh and other Japanese traditions. But film is the American tradition. In America it matured out of reference and stands on its own.
